title: Can Export Financing Help Countries Buy What They Need?
summary: See how export financing connects overseas equipment purchases with earlier vendor payments, using real cases and interactive tools to explore the trade-offs.
body_markdown:
Cover: Kotor, Montenegro. Photo by[Aleksandar Rusev](https://unsplash.com/@aegoplaces) /[Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/coastal-town-nestled-between-mountains-and-blue-bay-oGkY14DaAXE) . Illustrative location photograph.


A beach full of people streaming videos can become a financing problem surprisingly quickly.


The mobile network needs more capacity. The operator needs equipment. The equipment maker wants to get paid. But the money that pays for that investment comes in over years of people using the network.


Someone has to connect those timelines.


In Montenegro, Mtel is expanding its 5G network with Ericsson equipment.[EKN reports a €5.3 million Buyer Credit facility over 10 years](https://www.ekn.se/en/ekn-magazine/ekns-magazine/montenegros-5g-leap-how-swedish-export-finance-is-helping-mtel-meet-a-tourism-driven-data-surge/) , with Sweden’s SEK providing the loan and EKN guaranteeing it. The report was published in June 2026. It describes a transaction whose size attracted limited commercial-bank interest.


That is the interesting part: a country’s need for better infrastructure can be clear while the financing still takes some arranging.


## First, which kind of financing are we talking about?


Export Financing covers several tools. Receivables Financing turns unpaid invoices into earlier cash. Buyer Credit finances the overseas buyer’s purchase, with repayment spread over an agreed period. Export credit insurance covers specified non-payment risks. The[US Commerce Department’s Trade Finance Guide](https://www.trade.gov/report/trade-finance-guide) explains these different needs and structures.


The Montenegro deal addresses the buyer’s equipment purchase. The businesses providing components may have a separate need: getting paid soon enough to fund their next order.


**Explore the financing map below.** Follow the equipment, the payment and the guarantee separately. They do different jobs.


## What can the two countries get out of it?


For a smaller economy, access to equipment and the ability to pay for it can arrive together. For the exporting economy, financing can help turn overseas demand into an actual order.


Montenegro is an[upper-middle-income economy, according to the World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/montenegro) . That description is more useful here than treating every developing economy as if it has the same needs or borrowing capacity.


The cooperation can also involve several exporting countries. In 2024,[UKEF announced a €249 million loan for a Turkish solar project](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-and-poland-target-green-exports-with-249-million-financing-for-solar-project) , backed by its guarantee, with part of the exposure reinsured by Poland’s KUKE. British businesses were to provide electrical equipment; Polish businesses, security systems and steel components.


The project explorer shows the reported scale. Those are financing and design figures, rather than proof of electricity already delivered or development benefits achieved.


## The smaller businesses matter, too


A large project can still leave a small component maker waiting for payment.


There is already a model for addressing that. Under[US EXIM’s Supply Chain Finance Guarantee](https://exim.gov/solutions/working-capital/supply-chain-finance) , participating US vendors can sell qualifying invoices owed by a US exporter to a lender for early payment. EXIM provides a 90% guarantee on the eligible receivable; the lender retains 10% risk. Program requirements apply.


Our analysis: the opportunity is to plan both layers together. The overseas buyer gets financing suited to its investment. Businesses fulfilling the order get financing suited to their invoices. These can be separate facilities with different lenders and approval requirements.


## A longer repayment period still has a price


The calculator below lets you change the repayment period and see the annual payment alongside total interest. Try lowering the cash available for repayment, too.


A project can look affordable over a longer period while costing more overall. A guarantee can protect a lender against covered non-payment; the borrower still owes the debt.[EKN’s Buyer Credit Guarantee](https://www.ekn.se/en/guarantees/our-guarantees/ekns-guarantees/buyer-credit-guarantee/) describes that protection.


There is a real warning here.[UKEF’s 2024/25 annual report](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-export-finance-annual-report-and-accounts-2024-to-2025/uk-export-finance-annual-report-and-accounts-2024-to-2025) records that Ghana’s December 2022 debt suspension disrupted several supported projects. That is a historical example, not a claim about their status today.


So the useful question is bigger than whether financing is available. Can the buyer afford repayment after running costs, maintenance and a weaker year? Who covers delays? What happens if revenue and debt are in different currencies?


Export Financing can help countries trade equipment, technology and expertise on terms they can manage. Its most useful innovation may be quite simple: giving each business in the deal enough time to make the next step work.
